```{r}
library(tidyverse) 
library(dplyr)
library(corrplot)
```

```{r}
nhanes_merged <- read_csv("NHANES_20212023_merged_filtered 1.csv")
nhanes_codebook <- read_csv("NHANES_20212023_codebook_filtered 1.csv")

nrow(nhanes_merged)
ncol(nhanes_merged)
n_distinct(nhanes_merged$SEQN)
```
The dataset contained 11,933 observations and 486 variables. The participant identifier (SEQN) was unique for all observations, indicating that no duplicate participants were present in the dataset.

# How many samples and features are there, and what is each variable type (nominal, ordinal, continuous, discrete)?

What does the dataset look like? 
```{r}
glimpse(nhanes_merged)
```

After import, the majority of variables were stored as numeric (<dbl>), while a small number of variables were imported as character (<chr>) or logical (<lgl>) variables. However, NHANES frequently stores categorical variables using numeric codes (e.g. sex: 1 = male, 2 = female), meaning that the R storage type does not necessarily correspond to the underlying statistical variable type.

```{r}
names(nhanes_merged)[sapply(nhanes_merged, is.logical)]
``` 
```{r}
summary(nhanes_merged$BMIRECUM)
summary(nhanes_merged$BMIHEAD)
summary(nhanes_merged$LBXHCG)
summary(nhanes_merged$DBQ073D)
```
Four variables were imported as logical (<lgl>), namely BMIRECUM, BMIHEAD, LBXHCG and DBQ073D. Inspection showed that these variables contained exclusively or almost exclusively missing values and therefore contributed little information to the dataset.

```{r}
type_df <- tibble(
  variable    = names(nhanes_merged),
  is_num      = sapply(nhanes_merged, is.numeric),
  n_unique    = sapply(nhanes_merged, n_distinct, na.rm = TRUE),
  all_integer = sapply(nhanes_merged, function(x) is.numeric(x) && all(x == round(x), na.rm = TRUE))
) %>%
  left_join(nhanes_codebook, by = "variable") %>%
  mutate(type_guess = case_when(
    !is_num                      ~ "text / empty (non-numeric import)",
    n_unique == 2                ~ "binary (nominal)",
    n_unique <= 10 & all_integer ~ "categorical (nominal/ordinal)",
    all_integer & n_unique <= 30 ~ "discrete (count)",
    TRUE                         ~ "continuous"
  ))

table(type_df$type_guess)
```
An initial classification based on the number of unique values suggested the presence of 276 continuous variables, 98 binary variables, 88 categorical variables, 19 discrete variables and 5 text variables. Because NHANES stores many categorical variables as numeric codes, this classification was used only as a preliminary assessment and was subsequently verified using the codebook.

```{r}
nhanes_codebook[
  nhanes_codebook$variable %in%
    c("RIAGENDR",
      "RIDAGEYR",
      "DMDEDUC2",
      "DMDHHSIZ",
      "BMXBMI",
      "LBXTC"),
]
``` 
Variable types were subsequently verified using the NHANES codebook. Verification confirmed that the dataset contains a mixture of variable types. For example, gender (RIAGENDR) was classified as a nominal variable, education level (DMDEDUC2) as an ordinal variable, household size (DMDHHSIZ) as a discrete variable, and age (RIDAGEYR), body mass index (BMXBMI) and total cholesterol (LBXTC) as continuous variables. This confirms that the NHANES dataset contains a diverse range of variable types that require different statistical approaches in subsequent analyses.

Together, the automated classification and codebook verification showed that the dataset contains a combination of binary, nominal, ordinal, discrete and continuous variables, making it suitable for a wide range of statistical analyses.


```{r}
sort(table(nhanes_codebook$component),
     decreasing = TRUE)
```
Based on the NHANES codebook, variables were grouped into four main components: Laboratory (n = 387), Questionnaire (n = 40), Examination (n = 32) and Demographics (n = 27). The dataset is therefore largely composed of laboratory measurements.

# Where are the missing values, why might they be missing, should missingness be handled and how?
Missing values were not imputed; the justification is given after the selection of adults below."

```{r}
missing_pct <- colMeans(is.na(nhanes_merged)) * 100

summary(missing_pct)

sort(missing_pct, decreasing = TRUE)[1:20]
```
To quantify the extent of missingness, the percentage of missing values was calculated for each variable. Summary statistics and the variables with the highest levels of missingness were examined.


Missing values were common throughout the dataset. While some variables contained no missing observations, the median percentage of missing values per variable was 41.2% and the average percentage was 53.5%. Furthermore, 25% of all variables contained more than 75% missing data. Several variables exhibited nearly complete missingness (>99%), often because measurements were only collected for specific subpopulations. Therefore, missingness appears to be partly related to the NHANES study design rather than solely resulting from data quality issues.

To evaluate the potential impact of filtering, the number of variables exceeding different missingness thresholds was assessed.

```{r}
head(sort(missing_pct), 30)

sum(missing_pct > 75)
sum(missing_pct > 50)
sum(missing_pct > 25)
```
Applying different missing-value thresholds showed that 156 variables contained more than 75% missing data and 191 variables more than 50% missing data. This highlights the substantial amount of missingness present in the dataset and indicates that filtering and/or imputation strategies will need to be considered during preprocessing.

The distribution of missingness across all variables was visualised to investigate whether missing values were evenly distributed throughout the dataset.
```{r}
library(ggplot2)

missing_df <- data.frame(
  variable = names(nhanes_merged),
  missing_pct = colMeans(is.na(nhanes_merged)) * 100
)

ggplot(missing_df, aes(x = missing_pct)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of missing values across variables",
    x = "Percentage missing values",
    y = "Number of variables"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The histogram confirms that missingness is highly heterogeneous across variables, with many variables containing substantial proportions of missing observations.

```{r}
missing_df <- data.frame(
  variable = names(nhanes_merged),
  missing_pct = colMeans(is.na(nhanes_merged)) * 100
)

ggplot(missing_df,
       aes(x = reorder(variable, missing_pct),
           y = missing_pct)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Missingness per variable",
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Percentage missing values"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
```{r}
missing_df <- merge(
  missing_df,
  nhanes_codebook[, c("variable", "component")],
  by = "variable"
)

head(missing_df)
```

To investigate whether missingness differed across NHANES data domains, variables were grouped according to their codebook component and compared.

```{r}
ggplot(
  missing_df,
  aes(x = component,
      y = missing_pct,
      fill = component)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Missingness by NHANES component",
    x = "Component",
    y = "Percentage missing values"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

Because several NHANES measurements are only collected for specific age groups, missingness patterns were compared between adults and children.
```{r}
is_adult <- nhanes_merged$RIDAGEYR >= 20

cmp <- tibble(
  variable      = names(nhanes_merged),
  miss_adults   = colMeans(is.na(nhanes_merged[is_adult, ])) * 100,
  miss_children = colMeans(is.na(nhanes_merged[!is_adult, ])) * 100
) %>% filter(variable != "SEQN")

ggplot(cmp, aes(x = miss_adults, y = miss_children)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Missingness in adults versus children",
       x = "% missing in adults (>= 20 y)", y = "% missing in children (< 20 y)")
```
Missingness differed substantially between adults and children for a number of variables, supporting the hypothesis that participant eligibility criteria contribute to the observed missingness patterns.


Missingness was not uniformly distributed across the NHANES components. Demographic variables generally exhibited the lowest proportion of missing values and included several variables with complete data availability, whereas questionnaire variables showed the highest levels of missingness. Laboratory and examination variables displayed intermediate levels of missingness, although considerable variability was observed between individual measurements. This pattern is consistent with the NHANES survey design, in which demographic information is collected from nearly all participants, while many questionnaire items, examinations and laboratory measurements are administered only to specific target populations, participants attending the Mobile Examination Center (MEC), or selected subsamples. Consequently, a substantial proportion of the observed missingness is likely related to study design and participant eligibility criteria rather than data quality issues alone. As missingness appears to be associated with known and observed study characteristics, the observed pattern is more consistent with a Missing At Random (MAR) mechanism than with Missing Completely At Random (MCAR). However, the exact missingness mechanism was not formally tested and therefore cannot be determined with certainty.
Comparison of missingness between adults and children revealed clear differences for several variables, further supporting the conclusion that missingness is largely driven by participant eligibility criteria and study design rather than occurring completely at random.


Should missingness be handled? 

Given the substantial amount of missing data observed across the dataset, a missingness threshold of 75% was considered during preprocessing. Applying this threshold reduced the number of variables from 486 to 330, while retaining all 11,933 participants. As a result, 156 variables with very high levels of missingness were excluded from further consideration. This approach reduces the influence of sparsely populated variables while preserving the majority of the available information for subsequent analyses.

```{r}
nhanes_75 <- nhanes_merged[, missing_pct <= 75]

dim(nhanes_75)
```
```{r}
table(nhanes_codebook$component[
  nhanes_codebook$variable %in%
    names(nhanes_merged)[missing_pct > 75]
])
```
Applying a 75% missingness threshold reduced the number of variables from 486 to 330, resulting in the exclusion of 156 variables. Most excluded variables originated from the laboratory component (n = 115), followed by questionnaire variables (n = 24), examination variables (n = 12) and demographic variables (n = 5). This suggests that the threshold primarily removes highly specialised laboratory measurements and selected questionnaire variables with limited data availability, while retaining the majority of demographic and examination information

#thematic focus 
Given the large number of retained variables (n = 330), a thematic focus was necessary for subsequent analyses. We chose to focus on cardiometabolic health, as the dataset contained a combination of demographic variables, anthropometric measurements and laboratory biomarkers that are known to be associated with cardiovascular and metabolic disease risk. This theme is well represented within the NHANES dataset and provides suitable variables for multivariable modelling, multiple-testing analyses and machine-learning applications in later project stages

Within this cardiometabolic framework, age (RIDAGEYR), sex (RIAGENDR), BMI (BMXBMI), total cholesterol (LBXTC) and income-to-poverty ratio (INDFMPIR) were selected as candidate variables for further exploration. These variables are biologically relevant, commonly used in epidemiological research and potentially suitable for addressing multivariable research questions in the subsequent project parts.

are the variables present in the threshold dataset?

```{r}
c("RIDAGEYR",
  "RIAGENDR",
  "BMXBMI",
  "LBXTC",
  "INDFMPIR") %in% names(nhanes_75)
```
Because survey-specific missing-value codes such as 7 ("Refused"), 9 ("Don't know"), 77 and 99 may not be recognised as missing values by R, the variables selected for the planned cardiometabolic analysis were inspected individually. Age (RIDAGEYR), sex (RIAGENDR), body mass index (BMXBMI), total cholesterol (LBXTC) and income-to-poverty ratio (INDFMPIR) were examined to determine whether missingness was represented through explicit NA values or through hidden survey-specific codes.

```{r}
summary(nhanes_75$RIDAGEYR)

table(nhanes_75$RIAGENDR,
      useNA = "always")

summary(nhanes_75$BMXBMI)
table(is.na(nhanes_75$BMXBMI))

summary(nhanes_75$LBXTC)
table(is.na(nhanes_75$LBXTC))

summary(nhanes_75$INDFMPIR)
sort(unique(nhanes_75$INDFMPIR))
```
No hidden missing-value codes were identified in the selected cardiometabolic variables. Age and sex contained no missing values, while missingness in BMI, total cholesterol and income-to-poverty ratio was already represented through explicit NA values. Therefore, no additional recoding was required prior to further analyses.

```{r}
sel_vars <- c("RIDAGEYR", "BMXBMI", "LBXTC", "INDFMPIR")

adults <- nhanes_75 %>% filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20)

nrow(adults)
colSums(!is.na(adults[c(sel_vars, "RIAGENDR")]))
```
Because our research question will concern adults, all subsequent exploration was restricted to participants aged 20 years or older (n = 7,809). Children were excluded because several selected variables (e.g. BMI, total cholesterol and income-to-poverty ratio) are measured only in specific age groups or are not comparable between children and adults. The number of available observations per selected variable was BMI: 5,970; total cholesterol: 5,498; income-to-poverty ratio: 6,489.

```{r}
# Complete cases versus excluded adults: is the complete-case set comparable?
adults_check <- adults %>%
  mutate(complete = if_all(all_of(c(sel_vars, "RIAGENDR")), ~ !is.na(.x)))

adults_check %>%
  group_by(complete) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_age   = mean(RIDAGEYR),
            pct_female = mean(RIAGENDR == 2) * 100,
            mean_pir   = mean(INDFMPIR, na.rm = TRUE))

# Why are values missing? Interview only (RIDSTATR = 1) vs. interview + examination (2)
table(adults$RIDSTATR)
adults %>%
  group_by(RIDSTATR) %>%
  summarise(pct_with_cholesterol = mean(!is.na(LBXTC)) * 100)
```

Missing values were not imputed. First, much of the missingness is structural: 1,745 adults were interviewed but not examined (RIDSTATR = 1) and therefore have no BMI or cholesterol measurement, whereas 91% of examined adults have a cholesterol value; imputing a measurement that was never taken would create artificial data. Second, imputation methods such as mean or kNN imputation ignore the survey design and would add information for about 40% of the cholesterol values. Instead, each analysis uses complete cases for its own variables and reports the resulting sample size (n = 4,731 for the selected variables). To check that this does not introduce an obvious bias, the complete cases (4,731) were compared with the excluded adults (3,078): they were similar in age (53.9 vs 53.2 years) and sex (55.1% vs 55.6% female), with a slightly lower income-to-poverty ratio in the excluded group (2.98 vs 2.68). Results should nevertheless be interpreted with this limitation in mind.

#Are there samples or features that behave unlike the rest? Is that a technical error or interesting biology?

#Are there pre-processing steps needed on the data (normalization, log-transformation, standardization, filtering, etc)?

```{r}
iqr_out <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(.25, .75), na.rm = TRUE); i <- diff(q)
  sum(x < q[1] - 1.5 * i | x > q[2] + 1.5 * i, na.rm = TRUE)
}

sapply(adults[sel_vars], iqr_out)
sapply(adults[sel_vars], range, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(adults$INDFMPIR == 5, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(adults$RIDAGEYR == 80, na.rm = TRUE)
```
Among adults, the IQR rule flagged 173 BMI values and 77 total cholesterol values as extreme, but all remained within biologically plausible ranges (BMI 11.1–74.8 kg/m², total cholesterol 62–438 mg/dL) and were therefore considered genuine biological variation rather than technical errors. Two variables are top-coded by the survey: age (all participants ≥ 80 years are recorded as 80, n = 525) and the income-to-poverty ratio (values above 5 are recorded as 5, n = 1,616). 

```{r}
summary(adults$RIDAGEYR)
summary(adults$BMXBMI)
summary(adults$LBXTC)
summary(adults$INDFMPIR)
```
```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2,2))

hist(adults$RIDAGEYR,
     main = "Age")

hist(adults$BMXBMI,
     main = "BMI")

hist(adults$LBXTC,
     main = "Total cholesterol")

hist(adults$INDFMPIR,
     main = "Income-to-poverty ratio")
```
```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2,2))

boxplot(adults$RIDAGEYR,
        main = "Age")

boxplot(adults$BMXBMI,
        main = "BMI")

boxplot(adults$LBXTC,
        main = "Total cholesterol")

boxplot(adults$INDFMPIR,
        main = "Income-to-poverty ratio")
```
Histograms and boxplots showed moderate right-skewness for BMI and mild for total cholesterol and an accumulation of the income-to-poverty ratio at its upper limit (top-coding), but no implausible values; no observations were removed.

```{r}
# Skewness of the selected variables, before and after log-transformation
skew <- function(x) { x <- x[!is.na(x)]; mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))^3 }

sapply(adults[sel_vars], skew)
skew(log(adults$BMXBMI))
skew(log(adults$LBXTC))
```
```{r}
# Standardisation (z-scores): mean 0, SD 1, so that variables on different scales contribute equally
scaled_df <- adults %>%
  select(all_of(sel_vars)) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))))

bind_rows(
  adults %>% select(all_of(sel_vars)) %>% pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(stage = "Before standardisation"),
  scaled_df %>% pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(stage = "After standardisation")
) %>%
  mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = c("Before standardisation", "After standardisation"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = variable, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ stage, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Selected variables before and after standardisation",
       x = "Variable", y = "Value") +
  theme_minimal()
```
The selected variables are measured on very different scales (e.g. total cholesterol ≈ 188 mg/dL versus income-to-poverty ratio ≈ 2.9), so they were standardised to z-scores (mean 0, SD 1) for PCA and machine-learning analyses, to avoid variables with a large range dominating the variance. Skewness was 1.23 for BMI, 0.55 for total cholesterol and close to 0 for age and the income-to-poverty ratio. A log-transformation reduced the skewness of BMI to 0.42, but no transformation was applied: BMI is only moderately skewed, it remains interpretable in kg/m², and linear regression assumes normally distributed residuals rather than predictors. This assumption is checked in part 2, and a log-transformation will be reconsidered if the residuals deviate clearly from normality. Count-based normalisation as used for RNA-seq data is not applicable to these survey measurements.

Several preprocessing steps were applied. First, variables with more than 75% missing values were removed, reducing the dataset from 486 to 330 variables while retaining all 11,933 participants; the 75% cut-off lies in a cluster of variables from the same NHANES files that share the same missing participants, so the exact number of removed variables depends on the threshold. Second, all further exploration was restricted to adults (≥ 20 years). Third, hidden missing-value codes were assessed for the selected variables and did not require recoding. No outliers were removed. No transformation was applied because linear regression assumes normally distributed residuals rather than predictors, and this is checked in part 2. Finally, the selected variables are on different scales and are standardised (mean 0, SD 1) for PCA and machine-learning analyses. Missing values are not imputed: each analysis uses the complete cases for its own variables and reports the resulting sample size.

#Do samples cluster by the biology you care about, or by a technical factor?
```{r}
library(ggfortify)
pca_df <- adults %>%
  select(RIAGENDR, RIDEXMON, all_of(sel_vars)) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(
    sex    = factor(RIAGENDR, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    period = factor(RIDEXMON, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Nov-Apr", "May-Oct"))
  )

nrow(pca_df)

pca <- prcomp(pca_df %>% select(all_of(sel_vars)), scale. = TRUE)

round(summary(pca)$importance, 3)
round(pca$rotation[, 1:2], 2)
```

```{r}
autoplot(pca, data = pca_df, colour = "sex", alpha = 0.4,
         loadings = TRUE, loadings.label = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "PCA of adults coloured by sex")

autoplot(pca, data = pca_df, colour = "period", alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "PCA of adults coloured by examination period")
```

To investigate whether samples cluster by biological or technical factors, a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on 4,731 adults with complete data for age, BMI, total cholesterol and income-to-poverty ratio (standardised). The first two components explained 28.2% and 25.3% of the variance (cumulative 53.5%); the variance was spread almost evenly over the four components, indicating that the variables are only weakly correlated and that PCA compresses these data little. PC1 was driven mainly by the income-to-poverty ratio, BMI and total cholesterol, and PC2 mainly by age. Samples showed no clear separation by sex or by examination period, as the groups overlapped almost completely in the first two components. This suggests that neither factor is a dominant source of variation in these variables. A technical batch effect cannot be fully excluded, because information on laboratory batches or analysers is not available in the public NHANES data.


To explore potential relationships between the variables selected for the cardiometabolic framework, a correlation analysis was performed.
```{r}
corr_mat <- cor(adults[sel_vars], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
round(corr_mat, 2)

corrplot(corr_mat, method = "color", type = "upper",
         addCoef.col = "black", tl.col = "black")
```
A correlation analysis was performed on the selected continuous variables among adults. All pairwise correlations were weak (|r| ≤ 0.08): BMI correlated weakly negatively with the income-to-poverty ratio (r = −0.08) and total cholesterol (r = −0.04), and age was essentially uncorrelated with BMI and total cholesterol (r ≈ 0). No evidence of multicollinearity was found, so the variables provide largely distinct information for the subsequent multivariable analyses. When children were included, age and BMI correlated at r = 0.42, reflecting growth in childhood rather than an association in adults, which is why the analysis is restricted to adults.

# Is the preprocessed dataset suitable for the types of questions you want to answer in the next parts?

```{r}
analysis_df <- adults %>%
  select(SEQN, RIAGENDR, RIDEXMON, all_of(sel_vars))

nrow(analysis_df)
nrow(drop_na(analysis_df))

lab_vars <- nhanes_codebook %>%
  filter(component == "Laboratory", variable %in% names(adults)) %>%
  pull(variable)

miss_lab <- colMeans(is.na(adults[lab_vars])) * 100
sum(miss_lab <= 50)
```

After preprocessing, the dataset contains 7,809 adults (≥ 20 years) and 330 variables, of which the selected cardiometabolic variables (age, sex, BMI, total cholesterol and income-to-poverty ratio) are available for 4,731 participants. This is sufficient for a multivariable regression (part 2). For the multiple-testing study (part 3), 254 laboratory variables with at most 50% missing values are available in adults, well above the required 20 features; some of these are the same measurement in different units and will be reduced to one version per measurement. For the machine-learning application (part 4), the dataset contains both continuous and categorical variables that can be used as outcome and predictors. Missing values were not imputed; each analysis uses the complete cases for its own variables and reports the resulting sample size. Limitations are the cross-sectional design, the top-coding of age (80 years) and the income-to-poverty ratio (5.0), the lack of information on lipid-lowering medication, and the fact that NHANES survey weights are not used.

```{r}
# Save the preprocessed data so that parts 2-4 can start from here
saveRDS(adults, "adults_preprocessed.rds")     # all adults (>= 20 y), 330 variables
saveRDS(analysis_df, "analysis_df.rds")        # selected cardiometabolic variables only
```
